content: A burn is an injury that occurs due to exposure to heat, cold, electricity, chemicals, light, radiation, or friction. The extent of tissue damage, severity, and associated complications can vary significantly. Burns can affect multiple layers of tissue, including the epidermis, blood vessels, muscles, and even bones. Damage to nerve endings often results in significant pain. Depending on the location and severity of the burn, patients may experience life-threatening complications such as shock, infections, electrolyte imbalances, and respiratory distress. Additionally, burns can lead to profound psychological and emotional distress due to scarring and deformities. The history of burn injuries dates back over 3,500 years. In the 1500s, Ambroise Paré, a French barber-surgeon, was the first to classify burns into different degrees. However, for many decades, there was limited progress in understanding the pathophysiology of burns or developing effective treatments. In the 9th century, the Arabian physician Rhazes contributed to the early development of burn care. By the 1940s, significant advancements, such as skin grafting, were introduced to improve wound healing and restore body structure. The term burn injury was later formally adopted in medical nomenclature to describe a condition with characteristic symptoms, causes, and treatments. Burns are classified based on their severity into first, second, and third-degree burns. They can also be categorized by depth into superficial thickness, partial thickness, and full-thickness burns. The pathophysiology of burns involves damage caused by heat, cold, electricity, chemicals, light, radiation, or friction. The injury can vary in terms of tissue involvement, severity, and complications. Burns can damage the epidermis, blood vessels, muscles, and bones, often causing severe pain due to nerve damage. Depending on the burn's location and severity, complications such as shock, infections, electrolyte imbalances, and respiratory distress may arise. Psychological and emotional distress, including issues related to scarring and deformity, are also common. Burn injuries can result from various causes, including chemical exposure, friction, electrical injuries, radiation, extreme temperatures (both hot and cold), and inhalation injuries. Burn injuries are most commonly observed as thermal injuries, such as scalds, and are particularly prevalent in children and young adults. In the United States, approximately 1,344,100 individuals of all ages sustain burn injuries annually. The most affected age group is typically between 20 and 30 years old, with females being more frequently affected than males. Burn injuries are more common in individuals from lowand middle-income backgrounds and in low-income countries. Pulmonary complications, including those caused by inhalation injuries, account for up to 77% of burn-related deaths. If left untreated, burn injuries can progress from early stages to advanced complications, such as severe scarring and contractures. Common complications include infections, bedsores, post-burn seizures, hypertrophic scars, keloids, respiratory complications, and systemic complications. Treatment focuses on the burn's size and depth and may include fluid resuscitation, wound excision, grafting, infection control, and nutritional support. Burn injuries are diagnosed through a combination of patient history, symptoms, and physical examination. Symptoms can be divided into skin-related and airway-related categories. Physical examination involves assessing the thickness and total body surface area affected by the burn. Burns may occur on various body parts, including the head, neck, arms, legs, anterior trunk, posterior trunk, and genitalia. Laboratory findings are not specific to burn injuries but are used to assess the severity of the burn and its symptoms. Common tests include a complete blood count (CBC) to detect increased white blood cells (indicating infection or inflammation), decreased red blood cells (due to trauma), and elevated hematocrit levels (from fluid loss). Other findings may include elevated blood urea nitrogen (BUN) levels (indicating kidney damage) and decreased protein levels (due to protein loss through damaged blood vessels). Electrocardiograms (ECGs) have limited diagnostic value for burns but are useful for identifying conduction abnormalities and monitoring complications, particularly in electrical burns. ECG findings in acute burn injuries may include prolonged QT intervals and sinus tachycardia. Fatal cardiac arrhythmias can occur in cases of electrical weapon injuries. Imaging studies, such as chest X-rays, echocardiography, and CT scans, may be used to evaluate burn injuries. CT scans can reveal skin thickening, subcutaneous soft tissue changes, and damage to deeper structures such as fascia and muscle layers. CT imaging of the chest is particularly useful for assessing inhalation injuries and smoke inhalation. Treatment of burn injuries includes both medical and surgical approaches. Prevention strategies, such as education, engineering, and enforcement, are essential for reducing the incidence and severity of burns. Combining prevention and care strategies has significantly decreased burn-related mortality, reduced hospital stays, and improved outcomes for burn patients.
